{{Nihongo|'''Yusuke Nakamura'''|中村 祐輔|Nakamura Yūsuke|born 8 December 1952}} is a Japanese [[geneticist]] and [[cancer researcher]] best known for developing [[Genome-wide association study|Genome-Wide Association Study (GWAS)]]. He is one of the world's pioneers in applying [[genetic variations]] ([[Variable Number Tandem Repeat|Variable Number Tandem Repeat (VNTR)]] and [[Single-nucleotide polymorphism|Single Nucleotide Polymorphism (SNP)]] markers) and [[whole genome sequencing]], leading the research field of [[personalized medicine]].<ref name="bsd">{{cite web|url=http://med-www02.bsd.uchicago.edu/339/FacultyPro/faculty_profile.aspx?empl_id=13548|title=Yusuke Nakamura, Department of Medicine Faculty|access-date=2014-02-12|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140222143550/http://med-www02.bsd.uchicago.edu/339/FacultyPro/faculty_profile.aspx?empl_id=13548|archive-date=2014-02-22}}</ref>

==Scientific Contribution==
[[File:Yusuke Nakamura June 2012.jpg|thumb|left|200px|Yūsuke Nakamura]]
Nakamura successfully identified [[Variable Number Tandem Repeat|VNTR]] markers in 1987<ref>{{cite journal|pmid=3029872|year=1987|last1=Nakamura|first1=Y|title=Variable number of tandem repeat (VNTR) markers for human gene mapping|journal=Science|volume=235|issue=4796|pages=1616–22|last2=Leppert|first2=M|last3=O'Connell|first3=P|last4=Wolff|first4=R |last5=Holm|first5=T|last6=Culver|first6=M|last7=Martin|first7=C|last8=Fujimoto|first8=E|last9=Hoff|first9=M|last10=Kumlin|first10=E|doi=10.1126/science.3029872|bibcode=1987Sci...235.1616N}}</ref> and [[tumor suppressor gene]] ''APC'' in 1991.<ref>{{cite journal|pmid=1651562|year=1991|last1=Kinzler|first1=K. W.|author-link1=Kenneth W. Kinzler|title=Identification of FAP locus genes from chromosome 5q21|journal=Science|volume=253 |issue=5020|pages=661–5|last2=Nilbert|first2=M. C.|last3=Su|first3=L. K.|last4=Vogelstein|first4=B|last5=Bryan|first5=T. M.|last6=Levy|first6=D. B.|last7=Smith|first7=K. J.|last8=Preisinger|first8=A. C.|last9=Hedge|first9=P|last10=McKechnie|first10=D|doi=10.1126/science.1651562|bibcode=1991Sci...253..661K}}</ref> Furthermore, several genetic polymorphic markers developed and mapped by his research groups at the [[Japanese Foundation for Cancer Research]] and the [[University of Tokyo]], have contributed to map and clone genes responsible to [[hereditary diseases]], as well as those related to [[drug response]] and involved in [[cancer]].

In 2001, Nakamura and his colleagues of [[RIKEN|RIKEN SNP Research Center]] developed the methodology of [[Genome-wide association study|Genome-Wide Association Study (GWAS)]],<ref>{{cite journal|pmid=11501945|year=2001|last1=Ohnishi|first1=Y.|title=A high-throughput SNP typing system for genome-wide association studies|journal=Journal of Human Genetics|volume=46|issue=8|pages=471–7|last2=Tanaka|first2=T.|last3=Ozaki|first3=K.|last4=Yamada|first4=R.|last5=Suzuki|first5=H.|last6=Nakamura|first6=Y.|doi=10.1007/s100380170047|doi-access=free}}</ref> and using this method his research group first discovered functional SNP in the lymphotoxin-α gene that are associated with susceptibility to [[myocardial infarction]] in 2002, which was a breakthrough in the research field of [[medical genetics]].<ref>{{cite journal|pmid=12426569|year=2002|last1=Ozaki|first1=K.|title=Functional SNPS in the lymphotoxin-alpha gene that are associated with susceptibility to myocardial infarction|journal=Nature Genetics|volume=32|issue=4|pages=650–4|last2=Ohnishi|first2=Y.|last3=Iida|first3=A.|last4=Sekine|first4=A.|last5=Yamada|first5=R.|last6=Tsunoda|first6=T.|last7=Sato|first7=H.|last8=Sato|first8=H.|last9=Hori|first9=M.|last10=Nakamura|first10=Y.|last11=Tanaka|first11=T.|doi=10.1038/ng1047|s2cid=21414260}}</ref>

Furthermore, the RIKEN SNP Research Center led by him made the largest contribution in the Phase 1 HapMap project of the [[International HapMap Consortium]] published in the scientific journal [[Nature (journal)|''Nature'']] in 2005.<ref>{{cite journal|pmid=16255080|pmc=1880871|year=2005|author1=International HapMap Consortium|title=A haplotype map of the human genome|journal=Nature|volume=437|issue=7063|pages=1299–320|doi=10.1038/nature04226|bibcode=2005Natur.437.1299T}}</ref>

Nakamura focused on applying genetic information to improve the care of cancer patients, working to bring his laboratory's discoveries into the clinical practice.{{citation needed|date=October 2021}}

In 2001, his cancer research at the [[University of Tokyo]] led to the formation of OncoTherapy Science, a successful public Japanese biotechnology company that concentrates on new cancer therapies.{{citation needed|date=October 2021}}

==Life and career==
Nakamura was born in [[Osaka, Japan]] on 8 December 1952.<ref name=ims/> He received his medical degree in 1977 and his PhD in 1984 from [[Osaka University]]. While working as a [[surgeon]] in Japan, he witnessed a 27-year-old patient die of [[cancer]], which affected him deeply.<ref name="fet">{{cite web|url=http://www.uchospitals.edu/news/features/nakamura.html|title=I would like to cure cancer|access-date=2017-10-07|archive-date=2017-10-08|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171008030600/http://www.uchospitals.edu/news/features/nakamura.html|url-status=dead}}</ref>

To pursue advanced study in [[genetics]] and [[oncology]], he went to [[United States|the US]] and spent five years as a [[postdoctoral fellow]] and then as a [[faculty member]] at the [[Howard Hughes Medical Institute]] at the [[University of Utah]], an international center for [[gene mapping]].{{citation needed|date=October 2021}}

In 1989, Nakamura became Head of the Biochemistry Department, at the Cancer Institute, [[Japanese Foundation for Cancer Research]].<ref name="ims">[https://www.ims.u-tokyo.ac.jp/nakamura/main/ecv-naka.html Yusuke Nakamura MD PhD]</ref> He was appointed as [[Professor]] at the [[Institute of Medical Science (Japan)|Institute of Medical Science]], [[University of Tokyo]] in 1994. When the [[Government of Japan|Japanese government]] launched its Millennium Genome Project in 2000, he was named group leader for the genetic diversity program at the renowned RIKEN SNP Research Center. He also served as [[Director (business)|director]] of the RIKEN Center from 2005 to 2010, as well as Director of National Cancer Research Research Institute from 2010 to 2011.
From January to December 2011, he was Special Advisor to the Cabinet Secretary General, Office of Medical Innovation, Cabinet Secretariat, Government of Japan.<ref name=ims/>

In 2012, Nakamura moved to the Department of Medicine at the [[University of Chicago]] in 2012 as Professor and deputy director, Center for Personalized Therapeutics<ref name=ims/>

In 2018, after becoming the emeritus Faculty Professor of the [[University of Chicago]] and returning to Japan, he was appointed Director of Cross-ministerial Strategic Innovation Promotion Program of Japanese [[Cabinet Office (Japan)|Cabinet Office]], as well as Director at the Cancer Precision Center, Japanese Foundation for Cancer Research.{{citation needed|date=October 2021}}

==Awards==
Nakamura received several honors and awards include the following.
*1992: [[Princess Takamatsu|Princess Takamatsu Cancer Research Award]]
*2000: [[Keio Medical Science Prize]] for "Elucidation of various genetic diseases through human genome analysis"<ref>[https://www.ms-fund.keio.ac.jp/en/prize/005.html The 2000 Keio Medical Science Prize Awardees]</ref>
*2002: [[Tomizo Yoshida|Tomizo Yoshida Award]] of the [[Japanese Cancer Association]]
*2004: [[Medals of Honor|Japanese Medal of Honor with purple ribbon]]
*2010: [[Human Genome Organization|Chen Award for Distinguished Academic Achievement in Human Genetic and Genomic Research, Human Genome Organization (HUGO)]]<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.hugo-international.org/page-18074 |title=Chen Award for Distinguished Academic Achievement in Human Genetic and Genomic Research (2010) |access-date=2019-06-23 |archive-date=2019-06-23 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190623195140/http://www.hugo-international.org/page-18074 |url-status=dead }}</ref>
*2020: [[Clarivate Citation Laureate]]
